catalog_quote: [p. 216] These two differ in one regard: compensatory lengthening can occur in any syllable, while inherited length is never found on the ultima, and in most Bs dialects (except Mas, Sor, N-S, S-L, War) is restricted to the penult. All Bs speech varieties except some dialects of Kuy and Tsg retain phonemic accent. The following minimal pair is found in all dialects and establishes contrastive accent for PBS: púnuq [pú:nŭq] tree trunk < PBS *púnuq and punúq [pŭnúq] full < PBS *punúq. [p. 218] (1) CANONICAL FORM. In all Bs dialects studied, a closed penult is stressed. Thus, stress is predictable from the shape of the form: all dialects síŋsiŋ ring < PBS *síŋsiŋ, all dialects búkbuk weevil < PBS *búkbuk. Regardless of the accent on the base form, if morphophonemic changes produce a form with a CVC-penult, the penult is stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Semirara/Caluyanun, like all Bisayan varieties other than (some dialects of) Kuyonon and Tausug, has contrastive (phonemic) word accent: accent falls lexically on either the penult (realised with a long vowel in an open penult) or the final syllable (e.g. púnuq 'tree trunk' vs punúq 'full'); it is predictable only when the penult is closed (CVC), in which case the penult is stressed. Accent never falls earlier than the penult in West Bisayan.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (antepenultimate length stated to be lost in all Bs dialects outside the Waray group, sec. 10.2.3 p. 243).
new_statements.exceptions: Closed penult forces penult stress (also after affixation creates a CVC penult); historical *schwa in open penult yielded final accent; accent-shifting affix classes and form classes (nominative pronouns, deictics, interrogatives, numerals 1-9 tend to final stress, sec. 4.2.8 pp. 65-66, Sem forms cited: Sem qisará 'one', pirá 'how many'); word stress pattern can be overridden by exclamatory intonation (p. 50). Kuyonon (closest relative, same Kuyan subgroup) has LOST contrastive accent, so the retention in Sem is asserted by Zorc's explicit exclusion list, not by a Sem-specific paragraph.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic accent (length+stress) on citation forms across Zorc's 36-dialect Bisayan survey; Semirara is included by the 'all Bs speech varieties except Kuy and Tsg' scope and by Sem forms cited with penult vs final accent; Zorc's own Semirara worksheets (SEAlang, saved) mark accent on every form, both penult and final. Zorc also notes (p. 50) that 'stress is a syntactic feature.. it does not always coincide with length', i.e. length is the stable word-level correlate.
new_statements.identity_note: Zorc's 'Sem' = 'Semirara Is. dialect' (1977 p. xx; Table 2 no. 31 'Semirara (WBs), binisayáq, Semirara Island Group, data: full'), located by Zorc 1972 'on Semirara and Caluya islands' (Antique), Kuyan subgroup of West Bisayan with Kuyonon, Santa Teresa and Datagnon; his informant was from Bo. Semirara, Caluya, Antique. This is the language Glottolog calls Caluyanun [calu1238, ISO clu] (Glottolog's own classification comment cites Zorc 1977). Caution: the closest relative Kuyonon [cuyo1236/kuyo] is the Bisayan variety that LOST contrastive accent, so the Caluyanun value must not be copied from Kuyonon; Zorc's exclusion list names only Kuy and Tsg, leaving Sem among the accent-retaining varieties, and his Semirara worksheets show both penult- and final-accented forms.

sources.note: Primary data only, no prose rule. Every elicited form carries an acute accent, on either penult or final syllable (ano-final, sino-penult, ka?ino, di?in, basi?, pira, kamo, tana, isara-final, dato-final, indi?-initial, bala-final), i.e. Zorc transcribed contrastive accent for Semirara; note '/u-umlaut/ => [high central unrounded vowel]'. The earlier scan said this worksheet was not online; it is (SEAlang).

tone.quote: A phonological word is composed of a syllable bearing primary stress plus up to three pre-stress syllables and up to two post-stress syllables. Stress is phonemic, as is illustrated by the foolowing pairs of words: /pánit/ 'skin' /baníg/ 'mat' /dúto/ 'there' /dudá/ 'doubt' /ámo/ 'boss' /amó/ 'monkey' /bángalid/ 'slope' /ninunó/ 'ansistor'
